The search didn't turn up a current NREL figure for installed two-tank nitrate (solar salt) storage. The closest data points are older or refer to a different salt.

- **Chloride salt, NREL 2021:** A techno-economic study of molten chloride TES estimated the cost of the TES system at $60/kWhth, which is four times greater than Department of Energy targets. This concerns next-generation chloride salt, not the conventional two-tank nitrate system.
- **Conventional two-tank, 2004 study:** Herrmann, Kelly and Price concluded that the specific cost for a two-tank molten salt storage is in the range of US$ 30–40/kWhth depending on storage size. That figure is about 20 years old and predates current pricing.
- **DOE target:** A DOE program aimed to reduce the cost of Thermal Energy Storage (TES) to less than $15/kWh-th by 2020.
- **Gen3 goal:** The broader program targets an energy cost of 5 cents per kWh. That is a levelized energy cost, not a storage capex figure.
- **NREL cost model:** NREL has a capital cost methodology for TES, updated in 2011 for higher-temperature power cycles, which is the likely source for a bottom-up estimate. This report provides an update on the previous cost model for thermal energy storage (TES) systems.

For a current two-tank nitrate $/kWh figure, the next step would be to check NREL's recent CSP cost benchmarks or the 2024-era TES cost reports directly.

Links: [{"title":"Book a demo","url":"https://reonic.com/en-gb/blog/commercial-battery-storage-cost/"},{"title":"Why Commercial Battery Storage Systems Cost 40% Less in 2026: New Data Revealed","url":"https://dominionelectric.com/?p=3802"},{"title":"Why Commercial Battery Storage Systems Cost 40% Less in 2026: New Data Revealed","url":"https://dominionelectric.com/es/?p=3802"},{"title":"www.esource.com","url":"https://www.esource.com/printpdf/220477"},{"title":"C&I Battery Storage Costs Drop 40%","url":"https://mgrid.org/2025/12/08/commercial-battery-storage-costs-drop-40-percent-demand-charge-savings/"},{"title":"C&I Battery Storage Market Projects 5x Growth","url":"https://mgrid.org/?p=4939"},{"title":"C&I Battery Storage Costs Drop 40%","url":"https://mgrid.org/?p=4220"},{"title":"Battery Installation Cost 2026: What No One Tells You","url":"https://www.shop.bottegadelsarto.com/opinion/battery-installation-cost-2026-what-no-one-tells-you-179967"},{"title":"cost commercial battery storage economics roi analysis 2026 1422","url":"https://sustainableatlas.org/post/cost-commercial-battery-storage-economics-roi-analysis-2026-1422"}]

Most results put commercial and industrial (C&I) lithium-ion installed costs for 2025–2026 at roughly $180–$580/kWh, with the spread driven mostly by system size. The figures come from secondary industry blogs and vendor content, not primary datasets, so treat them as rough.

- **Size matters most:** One source puts installed lithium-ion BESS costs in 2025 at $180 to $300 per kWh for large containerized systems above 100 kWh and $280 to $580 per kWh for smaller commercial units. Another gives the same $280–$580 range for commercial units generally, noting that economies of scale can lower per-kWh costs for large projects.
- **Component-level estimate:** A breakdown for 4-hour LFP systems gives a total installed cost of $215 to $330/kWh. It also estimates a typical 500 kW/2 MWh commercial system at about $430,000 to $660,000 total, citing BloombergNEF for the broader trend.
- **Regional and UK figures:** One UK installer guide puts commercial storage at roughly £200 to £450 per kWh installed for a typical system, which is a different market and currency.
- **Caveats:** The sources don't agree. One reports a $50/kWh installation and connection adder on top of about $75/kWh core equipment, which implies much lower totals than the others. The lowest-cost figures cover large, DC-coupled or containerized systems, so they may not apply to a small site. Payback claims of 3–5 years depend on demand-charge structures and incentives, and one source notes a federal ITC covers 30% of installed costs, which may have changed since it was written.

I'd recommend checking NREL's Annual Technology Baseline or BloombergNEF's battery price survey for primary numbers before relying on these.

content.text:
## Building it up from the unit level

**Define the system:** two-tank molten-salt TES, solar salt (60/40 NaNO₃/KNO₃), ~290°C cold / ~565°C hot (ΔT≈275°C), sized for 5 MWh_th, cycled once/day.

**1. Salt inventory.** cp ≈ 1.5 kJ/kg·K → specific energy = cp·ΔT ≈ 412 kJ/kg ≈ 0.115 kWh_th/kg. For 5,000 kWh: mass ≈ 43,000 kg (~43 t). At ~$1,200/t → **≈$52,000** (~$10/kWh).

**2. Tanks.** Salt density ~1,900 kg/m³ → ~23 m³ of salt; each tank sized with ullage to hold the full inventory (~28 m³ each). Cold carbon-steel tank at ~$800/m³ ≈ $22,000; hot tank (refractory-lined or high-temp alloy, foundation cooling) at ~$2,500/m³ ≈ $70,000. **≈$92,000**.

**3. Insulation.** High-temp multilayer on a small vessel (~50 m² hot tank surface) plus heat-traced piping: **≈$35,000–40,000**.

**4. Molten-salt pumps.** These are the classic small-scale cost trap — custom cantilever pumps for hot corrosive salt have a cost floor largely independent of the tiny flow rate here. Hot + cold pump skids: **≈$100,000–120,000**.

**5. Charging (electric immersion heater, sized for ~4 h charge → 1.25 MW):** high-temp salt-rated elements at ~$200/kW → **≈$250,000**.

**6. Discharge heat exchanger** (salt-to-working-fluid, corrosion-resistant, ~1.25 MW): ~$250–300/kW → **≈$300,000**.

**Equipment subtotal ≈ $830,000–870,000.**
Add balance-of-plant (piping, valves, structural, electrical, controls, foundations) at ~40% of equipment: **+~$340,000**.
Add EPC/engineering/contingency at ~30%: **+~$360,000**.

**Total installed ≈ $1.5–1.6M → ≈$300–320/kWh of storage capacity.**

## Cross-check against real anchors

- Mature utility-scale two-tank nitrate systems (hundreds of MWh, CSP plants) run **~$20–40/kWh_th** installed; DOE's target was <$15/kWh_th.
- A 5 MWh system is ~100–200× smaller than a typical CSP tank farm. Using the standard capacity-cost scaling exponent (~0.6, i.e., cost/unit ∝ capacity^–0.4): (200)^0.4 ≈ 6.6× penalty → **$130–260/kWh_th** at 5 MWh.

That bracket (~$150–320/kWh_th) brackets my bottom-up number, which sits toward the high end because pumps, heaters, and the heat exchanger are "must-have" lumpy items that don't shrink proportionally with capacity. **Central estimate: ~$250–300/kWh_th installed for a standalone 5 MWh system.**

## Amortized cost of heat delivered

Assume 30-year life, ~1 cycle/day (≈300 effective cycles/yr after downtime), ~95% round-trip thermal retention, 7% discount rate (CRF ≈ 0.081), O&M ≈ 2.5%/yr of capex.

- Annual capital charge: $1.55M × 0.081 ≈ $126,000
- Annual O&M: ≈ $39,000
- Annual heat delivered: 300 × 5,000 kWh × 0.95 ≈ 1,425,000 kWh_th

**Levelized cost ≈ $165,000 / 1,425,000 kWh ≈ $0.12/kWh_th delivered** (roughly 10–15¢/kWh). Molten salt's cycle life isn't really "cycle-limited" the way batteries are — degradation is driven by pump wear, corrosion, and insulation life, not charge/discharge count, so 10,000+ cycles over 30 years is routine.

## Is it competitive with Li-ion? Depends what "delivered" means.

**If the product you want is heat** (process heat, district heat): there's effectively no efficient battery equivalent. Converting stored electricity (even cheap Li-ion electricity) back to heat via a resistive element is ~100% efficient, so Li-ion + heater is a real competitor on paper — but it only wins if the *input* to the thermal store would otherwise have to be purchased electricity. Molten-salt TES's actual advantage shows up when the input is already thermal and free/cheap (concentrated solar flux, waste heat, curtailed renewable electricity at large scale) — that's exactly the CSP use case, and at CSP scale ($20–40/kWh_th) it's far cheaper than buying and cycling a battery.

**If the product you want is electricity** (a "Carnot battery": charge via resistive heater, discharge via turbine/ORC): round-trip efficiency is capped by Rankine/ORC conversion at this temperature, realistically **30–45%**, and you still need to add power-block capex (turbine/generator, ~$1,000–2,000/kW) on top of the storage cost above — which at 5 MWh scale can rival or exceed the storage cost itself. Folding that in:
- Effective $/kWh of *electricity* capacity roughly triples (storage + power block, divided by a smaller electric-equivalent capacity).
- Levelized cost of *delivered electricity* lands around **$0.25–0.40+/kWh**.

Against that, a 5 MWh Li-ion BESS today installs for roughly **$200–300/kWh** (confirmed by current market data, lower end for larger containerized systems), with **90%+ round-trip efficiency** and comparable or better calendar/cycle life — giving a levelized electricity cost in the **$0.04–0.08/kWh** range.

**Verdict:** At 5 MWh scale, molten-salt TES is *not* cost-competitive with lithium-ion for electricity-in/electricity-out storage — it loses on both capital cost per usable kWh and round-trip efficiency. It only wins decisively where (a) the delivered product is heat rather than electricity, and (b) the input energy is already thermal rather than purchased electricity being converted twice — which is why molten salt TES is a CSP/industrial-heat technology, not a grid-battery substitute, and why it only gets genuinely cheap ($20–40/kWh_th) at 100–200× this scale.

Sources:
- [Technical and Economic Feasibility of Molten Chloride Salt Thermal Energy Storage Systems](https://research-hub.nrel.gov/en/publications/technical-and-economic-feasibility-of-molten-chloride-salt-therma-2/)
- [Developing a Cost Model and Methodology to Estimate Capital Costs for Thermal Energy Storage](https://research-hub.nrel.gov/en/publications/developing-a-cost-model-and-methodology-to-estimate-capital-costs/)
- [Why Commercial Battery Storage Systems Cost 40% Less in 2026: New Data Revealed](https://dominionelectric.com/?p=3802)
- [C&I Battery Storage Costs Drop 40%](https://mgrid.org/2025/12/08/commercial-battery-storage-costs-drop-40-percent-demand-charge-savings/)
